newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Gold price fall gives Australian mines the jitters.
newsitem.headline: Gold price fall gives Australian mines the jitters.

text.p: The latest slump in gold prices is giving Australia's army of gold companies the jitters, particularly those yet to mine a single ounce of the metal.
For scores of junior mining companies and hopeful prospectors pegging remote swathes of the Australian outback, exploration funding is the key to their success.
It can take years to bring a mine into production and exploration bills can soar into the millions, with no guarantee of finding a mother lode.
A steady, or better yet rising, gold price makes funding of gold mines more palatable to investors, while a falling price has just the opposite effect, the miners say.

Analysts warn that gold may be in for a rough ride this year, falling further out of favour among portfolio managers as alternative investments are presented to financial experts anxious to benefit from low inflation and unemployment.

In part owing to a fall in gold prices, Australia's earnings from gold exports will slip by 4.6 percent to A$5.4 billion in 1996/97 (July-June), the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics predicted last month.
But that prediction was based on an expected gold price for the year of US$379 an ounce, US$20 more than it is now fetching. Australia is the world's third-largest producer of gold.
In the first days of 1997, the precious metal took a lashing in international markets, hitting a three-year low of US$358.50.
The world's central banks, which hold about 35,000 tonnes of gold, could finally be ready to unload some of their hoard, pushing prices down even further.
And that would be particularly worrying for explorers, the fastest-growing sector of Australia's mining industry last year.
"The biggest impact from the gold price is on the capital raising potential," said Peter Ingram, chairman of Glengarry Resources NL, which is exploring prospects across Australia.
"For companies that are cashed up, a falling gold price is not a short-term problem...it's only a problem if it goes on," Ingram added.
Unlike early in 1996, when it soared above US$410 an ounce, gold has been a disappointment so far this year, losing about US$10 in value to hit a three-year low of US$358.50 an ounce.

For those miners already in production, hedging, or selling gold to be mined in the future for a fixed price higher than the current price, provides some protection from the cyclical whims of the marketplace.
"Larger companies are hedged because they have to fund longer-life mines," says Steve Dean of Camelot Resources NL.

Banks are anxious to guarantee the miners higher prices in order to get their hands on the gold and "lease" it back to the market with interest. Their risk is then diluted via complex options programmes and hedging bookings in currency markets.

But big mining houses suffer too when gold prices tumble. The Australian Stock Exchange's gold index of leading miners fell some five percent in two days this week as investors deserted mining stocks.
